summary:
Understanding Earth's changing surface requires more than what our eyes can see. Satellite radar technology offers a different perspective, revealing environmental changes even through clouds and darkness.

Wave of Change is an interactive educational experience that introduces users to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and its role in observing changes across land and water systems.

Guided by Sara, users explore how SAR works by sending microwave signals and measuring the energy scattered back toward a satellite. Through radar simulations and before-and-after image comparisons, they learn to interpret observations, identify potential changes, and recognize uncertainty.

The experience also highlights the limitations of radar observations, including the effects of buildings, vegetation, and observation timing.

Beyond understanding the technology, users explore how SAR data can support flood extent mapping, disaster warning efforts, and future flood planning when combined with other relevant evidence.

Our goal is to make satellite radar technology accessible and demonstrate how scientific observations can contribute to environmental awareness and informed decision-making.

WAVE OF CHANGE

Understanding Floods Through Synthetic Aperture Radar

1. Introduction and Problem Statement

Flooding is one of the most destructive natural hazards, affecting communities, infrastructure, agriculture, and livelihoods worldwide. During severe weather events, persistent cloud cover often limits the effectiveness of conventional optical satellite imagery, making it difficult to monitor affected areas when timely information is most needed.

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) offers an alternative approach to Earth observation. By using microwave signals instead of visible light, SAR can acquire observations through clouds and independently of daylight. This makes it particularly valuable for monitoring surface changes during floods.

However, interpreting radar imagery is not always straightforward. Changes in radar backscatter do not necessarily indicate flooding, and incorrect interpretations can lead to misleading conclusions.

2. Project Objective

Dancing with the SARs aims to make satellite radar technology more accessible through an interactive, case-based educational experience.

Our goal is to help users understand how SAR works, explore real satellite observations, identify potential surface changes, evaluate supporting evidence, and recognize the uncertainties involved in flood monitoring.

Rather than simply presenting a finished flood map, the experience encourages users to think like analysts and make evidence-based decisions.

3. Scientific Background

SAR is a remote-sensing technology that transmits microwave signals toward Earth's surface and records the energy scattered back toward the satellite.

The returned signal, known as backscatter, varies depending on surface characteristics such as roughness, moisture, geometry, and vegetation.

Open, relatively calm water often produces weak radar returns and appears dark in SAR imagery. However, this response can vary depending on environmental conditions and surrounding features.

By comparing radar observations acquired at different times, researchers can identify potential changes in land and water systems. These observations can support flood extent mapping, environmental monitoring, and disaster assessment.

4. Interactive Experience and Project Features

The website guides users through a series of interactive activities:

  • Hidden in Plain Sight: Introduces the limitations of optical imagery and demonstrates the value of radar observations.
  • Follow the Signal: Explains how radar signals interact with dry ground and water surfaces.
  • Change Detection: Allows users to compare radar observations and identify potential changes.
  • Evidence Evaluation: Encourages users to examine additional information before interpreting uncertain observations.
  • Understanding Uncertainty: Demonstrates why radar changes cannot automatically be classified as flooding.
  • Choose the Next Step: Explores how observations can support practical flood-response decisions.

The experience concludes with a personalized briefing based on the user's observations, evidence checks, and decisions.

5. Satellite Data and Case Studies

The project incorporates observations from multiple Earth-observation sources.

Sentinel-1 — Cyclone Amphan, Bangladesh (May 2020)

We use Sentinel-1 C-band radar observations from 16 and 22 May 2020 to explore flood-related changes associated with Cyclone Amphan. The case includes VV and VH polarizations and a published inundation dataset as a reference for comparison.

The comparison also demonstrates an important limitation: radar-based candidate detections do not necessarily correspond to confirmed flooded locations.

NISAR — Haor Basin, Bangladesh (June–November 2026)

Using NISAR L-band GCOV observations, we examine seasonal water-surface changes across the Haor Basin.

Across a study window measuring approximately 109 × 120 km, estimated open-water coverage reached 6,086 km² on 24 July 2026 and decreased to 3,584 km² by 9 November 2026.

This represents a decrease of approximately 2,502 km² from the observed peak. The analysis uses an HV backscatter threshold of −20 dB, and sensitivity testing demonstrates how changing the threshold affects the estimated water area.

NISAR — Tibetan Lakes (October–November 2026)

We also examine three lakes on the Tibetan Plateau to demonstrate that radar backscatter changes can occur even when a location is not experiencing flooding.

Across observations from 28 October to 9 November 2026, one lake increased in HH backscatter by 1.0 dB, another decreased by 3.9 dB, while Siling Co remained within 0.3 dB.

These observations demonstrate why changes in individual radar channels must be interpreted carefully and supported by additional evidence.

Nepal Flood Observation

The introductory Nepal flood scene uses an optical satellite image from 26 August 2026. It illustrates the challenge of observing flood-affected areas under cloud cover; it is not presented as a direct SAR observation.

6. Data Analysis and Methodology

Our analysis involves discovering satellite acquisitions, selecting suitable temporal observations, processing radar data, comparing backscatter values, and generating geospatial visualizations.

The wider NISAR analysis pipeline automates several stages:

  1. Discovering available NISAR L-band GCOV acquisitions.
  2. Selecting suitable temporal image pairs based on acquisition characteristics and spatial overlap.
  3. Downloading and processing satellite data.
  4. Comparing backscatter values across observation dates.
  5. Identifying candidate surface changes.
  6. Generating georeferenced maps, statistics, visualizations, and research reports.

The analysis uses conservative terminology: detected changes are treated as candidate flood-related changes rather than confirmed flooding unless independent validation is available.

7. Scientific Limitations

SAR is powerful, but its observations require careful interpretation.

  • Buildings and vegetation can influence radar backscatter.
  • Surface roughness and moisture can produce changes unrelated to flooding.
  • Observation timing and processing differences can affect comparisons.
  • Threshold-based water estimates are sensitive to the selected threshold.
  • Independent reference datasets are necessary to validate candidate flood detections.

Our project highlights these limitations to encourage responsible interpretation rather than presenting every detected change as a confirmed environmental event.

8. Real-world Applications and Impact

SAR observations can contribute to several important applications:

  • Flood extent mapping and monitoring.
  • Identifying potentially affected communities and infrastructure.
  • Supporting disaster response and situational awareness.
  • Monitoring seasonal changes in wetlands and other water systems.
  • Supporting environmental assessment and future planning.

Reliable decision-making requires combining radar observations with additional information, including optical imagery, river levels, weather forecasts, and local reports.

9. Technical Implementation

The project consists of an interactive web application and a separate NISAR data analysis pipeline.

The web application uses TypeScript, React, and Vite, while the analysis workflows use Python and geospatial processing libraries.

Together, these components connect scientific data processing with an accessible, interactive learning experience.

10. Future Scope

Future development could include additional geographical case studies, expanded satellite datasets, improved independent validation, and more extensive temporal analysis.

We also aim to make the learning experience more useful for students, researchers, and communities interested in understanding how satellite observations can contribute to environmental monitoring.

11. GitHub Repositories

Our project includes two complementary repositories, providing access to the data analysis pipeline and the interactive web application's source code.

1. NISAR Data Analysis Pipeline — Maha

A Python-based workflow for discovering, processing, and analyzing NISAR satellite observations, including temporal backscatter comparisons and geospatial visualizations.

Repository: https://github.com/Maha123b/nisar-analysis

2. Interactive Web Application — Onsae

The source code for Dancing with the SARs, including its interactive learning experience, radar simulations, and satellite data visualizations.

Repository: https://github.com/onsae09/nasa-spaceapp

## Team Contributions

Minjae Kim & Lily: Project Planning, Coordination, Documentation, and Submission.

Maha, Lude & Marshad: SAR Data Analysis and Scientific Research.

Onsae: Web Development, Coding, and Interactive Experience Implementation.

Conclusion

Dancing with the SARs connects satellite radar science with real environmental observations through interactive learning and data analysis.

By encouraging users to examine evidence, question uncertainty, and understand the limitations of remote sensing, the project demonstrates how scientific observation can contribute to better environmental awareness and more informed flood-related decision-making.
